There are 17 possible configurations.

**Setup.** Each pair is friends only, enemies only, or both. The first rule says the "friends" relation (including frenemies) is transitive. It is also symmetric, so it splits the five people into friend-classes. Every pair in different classes is therefore enemies only.

**Three or more classes are impossible.** Take A, B, C in three different classes. Then A–B and B–C are enemies, so the second rule forces A and C to be friends. That contradicts them being in different classes.

**Two classes X and Y.**
- Suppose two people A and A′ in X were enemies as well as friends. Take B in Y. Then A′–A and A–B are both enemy pairs, so A′ and B would have to be friends. They are in different classes, so this is a contradiction. Hence there are no frenemies.
- With no frenemies, the three rules hold. Two people in the same class are friends only, and anyone in the other class is their enemy only. The second rule holds because enemies in different classes, B–A and A′–B, have A and A′ in the same class, hence friends. The third rule holds because friends A, A′ and an enemy B give A–B enemy.
- The number of ways to split five people into two nonempty classes is S(5,2) = 15.

**One class (everyone is friends).**
- Suppose some pair A, B are also enemies. For any other person C, B–C are friends and B–A are enemies, so the third rule makes A–C enemies. The same argument then makes every pair enemies.
- So the only options are "all friends only" or "all frenemies". This gives 2 configurations.

**Total:** 15 + 2 = 17.

ANSWER: 17
